title: WHO Warns Global Cancer Cases Will Nearly Double to 35 Million by 2050

Key Takeaways
  • Global cancer cases are projected to reach 35 million annually by 2050.
  • Asia accounts for over half of the global cancer burden.
  • By 2050, the global cost of cancer could exceed $33.2 trillion.
  • Only 12 countries are on track to reduce premature cancer deaths by 2030.
  • The rise in cancer cases is linked to aging populations and worsening risk factors.

Cancer diagnoses worldwide are projected to climb to a staggering 35 million annually by 2050, up from 20.6 million in 2024, the World Health Organization warned in a sweeping new report that lays bare the growing inequities in cancer prevention and care across the globe.

The Scale of the Crisis

The WHO's latest global status report on cancer paints a sobering picture. About one in five people will develop cancer in their lifetime. Cancer remains the second leading cause of death worldwide after heart disease, with approximately one in nine men and one in thirteen women dying from the disease before age 75.

The most common cancers for men are lung and prostate cancer; for women, breast and lung cancer. Colorectal cancer ranks third for both sexes. Currently, there are an estimated 20.6 million new cases and 10 million deaths from cancer every year.

"The inequities documented in this report are not inevitable; they are the consequence of choices, and they can be reversed through stronger and unified action," said Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO's director-general.

Asia Bears the Heaviest Burden

Asia accounts for more than half of the global cancer burden, a figure driven partly by the fact that 60 percent of the world's population lives on the continent. Europe carries a disproportionately high share at 21 percent, followed by North America at 11 percent.

The numbers are particularly alarming for South Asian populations. India alone records over 1.4 million new cancer cases annually, with oral, cervical, and breast cancers among the most prevalent. Access to screening, early diagnosis, and affordable treatment remains severely limited in much of the subcontinent. Only 12 countries worldwide are on track to reduce premature cancer deaths by a third by 2030, while 48 countries have rising death rates.

Why Cases Are Rising

The surge is driven by a toxic mix of ageing populations and worsening risk factors. More than half of all cancer cases occur in people aged 65 and older, and by 2050 the proportion of the global population over 60 will nearly double compared to 2015. Meanwhile, while tobacco use has declined, other risk factors — alcohol consumption, obesity, physical inactivity, and air pollution — are either stagnant or worsening.

"The cancer profile is evolving, increasingly driven by rising rates of obesity, physical inactivity, unhealthy diets and air pollution," said Dr. Elisabete Weiderpass, director of the International Agency for Research on Cancer.

The Diaspora Dimension

For the Indian diaspora, the report carries particular relevance. Studies have consistently shown that South Asians carry elevated risks for certain cancers, including oral, stomach, and cervical cancers. Diaspora communities in the UK, US, Canada, and the Gulf often face barriers to screening due to language, cultural factors, and awareness gaps — even in countries with universal healthcare.

Economic Impact of Cancer
›Projected global cost by 2050: $33.2 trillion
›50% of patients face catastrophic health expenditures
›Up to 90% abandon treatment in low-income settings

The economic toll is equally devastating. By 2050, the cumulative global cost of cancer is projected to surpass $33.2 trillion — roughly equivalent to the entire GDP of the United States. About half of patients and their families experience catastrophic health expenditures, and in some low-income settings, up to 90 percent of patients abandon treatment entirely due to cost.

The WHO report calls for comprehensive, integrated approaches rather than disease-specific interventions, urging governments to invest in prevention, early detection, and equitable access to affordable treatment — particularly in low- and middle-income countries where the crisis is deepest.
